summaries.example: Imagine one particular apple. The apple itself is a primary substance: it is a thing that can exist on its own. Its redness is present in the apple, so it is an accidental particular. The kind “apple” can be said of many individual apples, making it like a secondary substance. The general idea “red” can also be said of many things, but redness is not essential to each one.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Categories explores how to sort everything we talk about into very broad kinds. One part of the work uses two questions: Is this thing said of another thing, as a general kind is said of many individuals? Is it present in another thing, as a color may be present in an object? These questions make four groups. An individual horse is a primary substance because it is neither said of nor present in something else. A general kind such as “horse” is said of individuals but is not present in them. A particular color is present in an object but is not said of many objects in the same way. A general quality such as “white” may be said of many things and present in them as a quality. Aristotle then gives a second system: ten categories for the most general kinds of things or predicates. The entry explains that scholars disagree about whether these categories are mainly about words, concepts, things in the world, or connections among all three. It also examines several proposals for how Aristotle might have formed the list. The work is important not because every part is settled, but because it gave later philosophy a powerful starting point for asking what kinds of things exist.
key_ideas: Aristotle uses two ways to sort beings: whether something is said of another thing and whether it is present in another thing.
The four resulting groups are accidental universals, essential universals, accidental particulars, and primary substances.
Primary substances, such as individual people and animals, are treated as the most basic beings.
Aristotle also gives ten very general categories, including substance, quantity, quality, relatives, place, time, position, having, acting, and being acted upon.
Philosophers disagree about exactly what Aristotle’s categories classify and how he arrived at his list.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Categories teaches us to notice that different kinds of features belong to things in different ways. It also shows why making a complete list of kinds is difficult. The questions Aristotle raised—about objects, properties, language, and reality—continued to influence philosophers long after him.

important_terms.definition: A basic way of sorting things. Aristotle proposed ten very general kinds, such as substance, quantity, quality, and relation.
An individual thing that can exist on its own, such as one particular horse or person.
A general kind or type that can be said of many individual things, such as “human” or “horse.”
A feature that belongs to something but is not what that thing essentially is, such as a color or a temporary position.
A general word or kind that applies to many things.
An individual thing, rather than a general kind.

questions_to_think_about: Is a thing’s color part of what the thing is, or is it an added feature?
What is the difference between one particular dog and the general kind “dog”?
Should words, ideas, or things in the world be placed into categories?
How could someone test whether a list of categories is complete?

summaries.example: Consider Socrates’ whiteness. On the standard interpretation discussed in the entry, Socrates is a primary substance: an individual, non-accidental being that is neither said-of nor present-in another. His particular whiteness is an accidental particular because it depends on being in Socrates and is not predicated of many subjects. The universal “white” is an accidental universal: it can be predicated of many substances, while being accidental to each. The universal “human,” by contrast, is a secondary substance: it is predicated of individual humans and expresses their essential kind.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Categories presents two central classificatory systems. The first divides beings by two relations: being said-of something and being present-in something. A widely adopted interpretation treats the first as a distinction between universals and particulars and the second as a distinction between accidental dependence and non-accidental status. On that reading, primary substances are individual, non-accidental beings such as a particular human or horse; secondary substances are essential universals such as human; accidental particulars are dependent instances such as one object’s whiteness; and accidental universals are repeatable qualities such as white. The entry emphasizes that this interpretation is useful but not definitive. Aristotle does not clearly define said-of, and his account of present-in may be circular or rely on an unexplained notion of being in. A later debate, associated with G. E. L. Owen, challenges the existence of non-substantial particulars and therefore rejects the usual mapping of the four groups onto universals and particulars. Aristotle’s second system divides what is said—or perhaps what words refer to—into ten highest kinds: substance, quantity, relatives, quality, place, time, position, having, acting, and being acted upon. The entry examines whether these are categories of language, concepts, reality, or predicates considered in relation to reality. It also discusses puzzles within quantity, relatives, and quality, and asks how Aristotle could justify the completeness of the list. Proposed answers appeal to patterns of questioning, grammar, modal relations, or later metaphysical derivations. None is presented as decisively established. key_ideas: The four-fold division combines said-of/not-said-of with present-in/not-present-in, yielding a structure of universals, particulars, essential kinds, accidents, and primary substances.
The standard interpretation identifies said-of with universality and present-in with accidental dependence, but Aristotle’s own formulations do not fully settle either technical relation.

The ten-fold division concerns the highest kinds, though scholars dispute whether its objects are linguistic predicates, concepts, worldly entities, or semantically structured connections between them.
Substance has priority because other entities are presented as dependent on primary substances; this gives the scheme an anti-Platonic emphasis on concrete particulars.
Aristotle’s rejection of being as a genus helps explain why he posits ten highest kinds rather than one all-inclusive category.
The entry surveys four proposals for generating the list: questioning, grammar, modal requirements, and medieval derivation, while noting problems for each.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s framework makes a basic metaphysical challenge visible: before deciding what exists, we need some account of the kinds into which things fall and how those kinds relate. The Categories also connects language with ontology—the study of being—without making their relationship simple. Its unresolved puzzles helped shape later work by medieval and modern philosophers and continue to provide material for debates about substance, properties, universals, and classification.

important_terms.definition: Aristotle’s system of very general kinds. His familiar list contains substance, quantity, relatives, quality, place, time, position, having, acting, and being acted upon.
A relation in which a universal is predicated of something else; the entry presents this as a natural but debated interpretation.
A relation in which an entity exists in a subject, not as a part and not separately from that subject; Aristotle’s wording leaves its precise meaning unsettled.
An individual, non-accidental entity that is neither said-of nor present-in another; Aristotle’s examples include an individual human and a horse.
A universal substance-kind, such as human, predicated of primary substances and understood as essential to them on the standard interpretation.
A property or feature that depends on a subject but is not essential to its kind, such as a particular instance of whiteness.
A most general kind under which more specific kinds may be organized; Aristotle rejects being as one single genus and instead posits ten highest kinds.
A proposed method for generating Aristotle’s categories, ranging from questions and grammar to modal relations and medieval metaphysical derivations.

questions_to_think_about: If a category system is shaped by language, how can we know that language reflects reality rather than merely convention?
Does Aristotle’s account need non-substantial particulars such as an individual instance of whiteness?
Why might body seem to belong both to substance and to quantity, and what problem does that create?
Can a procedure for generating categories justify the categories, or could the procedure simply reproduce our starting assumptions?
Should a theory of categories classify things, concepts, words, or relations among them?

summaries.example: Think about a soccer ball. The ball itself is an individual thing, so it resembles Aristotle’s primary substance. Its exact shade of blue is a feature that depends on the ball and could change, so it resembles an accidental particular. The kind “soccer ball” or “ball” can apply to many objects, so it resembles a universal. If we say “round,” that quality may apply to many balls, but being round is not necessarily what makes each object the kind of thing it is.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s Categories asks how the things we discuss can be organized into broad kinds. Its first important system is a four-fold division based on two technical relations. Something may be said of another thing, as a general kind is said of many individuals, or it may not be said of another. It may also be present in something, as a color or piece of knowledge may depend on a subject, or it may not be present in something. A common interpretation therefore describes four groups: accidental universals, essential universals, accidental particulars, and primary substances. An individual horse is a typical primary substance. The kind horse is a secondary substance, since it can be said of individual horses. A particular instance of whiteness depends on an object, while the general quality white can apply to many objects. The source stresses that this interpretation is not completely secure. Aristotle does not clearly define said-of, and his explanation of present-in may not solve the problem. One modern scholarly debate questions whether accidental particulars should be included at all. Aristotle then presents a second system: ten categories that are meant to be the most general kinds. They include substance, quantity, quality, relatives, place, time, position, having, acting, and being acted upon. The source considers whether these categories are about language, concepts, objects, or the ways predicates connect language with the world. It also points out puzzles: some categories seem natural, while others seem difficult to classify, and some examples appear to fit more than one category. key_ideas: Aristotle’s four-fold division uses two distinctions: said-of versus not said-of, and present-in versus not present-in.
On a common interpretation, these distinctions separate universals from particulars and accidental features from non-accidental beings.
Primary substances are given a special role because other beings are described as depending on them.
The ten categories are supposed to be the broadest kinds, but it is debated whether they classify words, ideas, things, or relationships between language and things.
The list includes familiar kinds such as substance and quality, but also unusual ones such as having and being acted upon.
Scholars have proposed different ways Aristotle might have made the list, and the source does not treat one proposal as settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because classification is not just putting labels on shelves. A category system makes claims about what is basic, what depends on what, and how language connects with the world. Aristotle’s proposal has influenced many later philosophers, even when they changed or rejected parts of it. Studying its difficulties helps us see why organizing reality is a philosophical problem.

important_terms.definition: A broad way of classifying things. Aristotle’s second system contains ten highest kinds, including substance, quantity, quality, and relatives.
An individual thing that is not said of something else and does not exist in something else, such as one particular person or animal.
A general kind that can be said of many individual things and may describe what they essentially are.
A feature that belongs to a subject but is not essential to its identity, such as a temporary color or position.
Something general that can apply to many individual things.
Something individual and distinct, such as one person’s particular instance of a quality.
A way a word or phrase points toward something else, as in “larger than” or “related to.”
The study of what kinds of things exist and how they are structured.

questions_to_think_about: Is “blue” a thing, a word, an idea, or a feature of an object?
Why might Aristotle consider an individual horse more basic than the general kind “horse”?
Could one object belong to more than one category, or would that create a problem?
Do the structures of language reveal the structure of reality?
What would count as evidence that a list of categories is complete?
